content: The Number Needed to Harm (NNH) is an epidemiological metric that quantifies the number of patients who must be exposed to a specific risk factor in order to cause harm in one individual who would not have otherwise been harmed. It is mathematically defined as the inverse of the attributable risk. A lower NNH value indicates a more dangerous risk factor, as fewer individuals need to be exposed for harm to occur. NNH is conceptually similar to the Number Needed to Treat (NNT), but while NNT typically refers to the number of patients who need to receive a therapeutic intervention to achieve one beneficial outcome, NNH pertains to the number of patients exposed to a harmful factor or intervention to result in one adverse outcome. NNH calculations are based on comparing exposed and non-exposed groups and can be derived from raw data or data adjusted for confounding variables. A specific clinical endpoint must be defined for the calculation. If the probabilities of the endpoint occurring in the exposed group (p_exposure) and the non-exposed group (p_non-exposure) are known, the NNH is calculated as 1 / (p_exposure p_non-exposure). NNH is a critical tool in evidence-based medicine, aiding clinicians in determining whether the potential harms of a treatment outweigh its therapeutic benefits. For example, even if a drug has a low NNH (indicating a higher risk of harm), it may still be justified in certain clinical scenarios if the NNT (indicating the drug's benefit) is lower than the NNH. Worked Example: In a cohort study, individuals exposed to a risk factor (Exposure +) are followed over a period of time to observe whether they develop a specific disease or outcome (Disease +). A control group of individuals not exposed to the risk factor (Exposure -) is also followed for the same duration. The follow-up time is calculated as the number of individuals in each group multiplied by the number of years each individual is observed. This follow-up time is essentially a weighted average of the duration of observation for all participants. The incidence rate in the exposed group is calculated as the number of cases in the exposed group divided by the total follow-up time for that group. Similarly, the incidence rate in the non-exposed group is calculated as the number of cases in the non-exposed group divided by the total follow-up time for that group. To determine the relative risk, divide the incidence rate in the exposed group by the incidence rate in the non-exposed group. To calculate the attributable risk, subtract the incidence rate in the non-exposed group from the incidence rate in the exposed group. The NNH is then calculated as the inverse of the attributable risk, or 1 / (incidence_exposure incidence_non-exposure). For example, if the NNH is calculated to be 714, this means that for every 714 individuals exposed to the risk factor, one individual will develop the disease or outcome that would not have occurred otherwise.
